I think the most parsimonious reading of the manipulations is that physiologically relevant NSC reactivation is driven by Dilp2 that is secreted into the hemolymph and then reaches the brain by crossing the BBB.

Feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs and the peptide is secreted. Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB, so hemolymph-derived ligand can access the brain parenchyma/NSC niche. The fat body Imp-L2 overexpression is a systemic extracellular sink. Imp-L2 binds Dilp2 in the hemolymph and, because Imp-L2 itself crosses the BBB, it will also be able to bind any Dilp2 that has entered the brain extracellular space from the circulation. The key point is that Imp-L2 acts extracellularly. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 from IPCs to DRNs is largely intracellular in transit and at the site of delivery, and therefore is largely protected from an extracellular binding protein until and unless it is released. If a protected, intracellular retrograde pool were sufficient to drive reactivation, removal of the extracellular circulating pool by a fat body sink should not abolish reactivation. The fact that fat body Imp-L2 soaking hemolymph Dilp2 keeps NSCs quiescent despite feeding is therefore most naturally read as a requirement for extracellular, circulating Dilp2.

The glial Imp-L2 result is compatible with this. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and it also reduces IPC Dilp2 expression. That is exactly the feedback you expect if central Dilp2 signalling that maintains IPC output is supplied by circulating Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB and is now being sequestered in the brain. The reduction in IPC expression is a secondary consequence of loss of brain Dilp2 signalling, not evidence for a separate retrograde requirement that is independent of the circulating pool.

DRN inhibition delays reactivation, but the prompt explicitly allows DRNs to have a Dilp2-independent function. Inhibition therefore establishes a requirement for DRN activity, not that Dilp2 must be retrogradely delivered to DRNs to act. The in vitro rescue with very high bovine insulin shows that direct insulin/Dilp signalling in brain tissue is sufficient in principle to drive reactivation, consistent with a model in which ligand arriving from the circulation is the physiological driver.

In short, the extracellular sink experiments remove accessible circulating Dilp2 and the phenotype is lost, whereas the retrograde pool would be largely inaccessible to that sink. The data therefore point to hemolymph-secreted Dilp2, crossing the BBB, as the source that drives feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core facts remain: Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, also retrogradely transported to DRNs, Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross BBB, Dilp2 mutant blocks exit from quiescence, fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent, glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation but DRNs may have a Dilp2-independent function, ex vivo very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation.

Two interpretive camps persist.

B camp: fat-body Imp-L2 is the decisive systemic necessity test. Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein; retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit / largely synaptic-private, so an extracellular sink should not neutralize it. The fact that a systemic extracellular sink abolishes feeding-induced reactivation therefore shows an extracellular accessible pool is required. Dilp2 crosses BBB so hemolymph-derived ligand can reach brain. Imp-L2 crossing BBB reinforces this: the sink removes Dilp2 from hemolymph and from the brain extracellular space that is fed by circulation. Glial Imp-L2 blocking reactivation and lowering IPC Dilp2 expression is read as loss of central Dilp2 signaling supplied from circulation feeding back to IPC output, not a separate retrograde requirement. DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2, explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent. In vitro high insulin shows ligand sufficiency for brain tissue.

E camp: Imp-L2 freely crosses BBB, so fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; it also delivers Imp-L2 into brain where it can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. The block is therefore compatible with loss of hemolymph, central, or both pools. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, so the phenotype can be secondary to feedback down-regulation of the source, lowering both hemolymph-secreted and retrograde pools together. With Dilp2 BBB-permeable, glial sequestration will also mop up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain. DRN inhibition is not diagnostic because DRNs may function independently of Dilp2 absorption. Ex vivo high insulin is supraphysiological bypass, shows sufficiency in principle not physiological route.

Unresolved issues: whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 is truly inaccessible to an extracellular Imp-L2 sink once released at DRN terminals; the causal direction of glial Imp-L2 → reduced IPC Dilp2 expression vs reduced IPC expression → NSC phenotype; whether free BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes any peripheral sink inherently central; no manipulation isolates hemolymph Dilp2 while sparing retrograde delivery, nor BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, nor IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport.

Disagreements centre on interpretability of Imp-L2 manipulations given BBB permeability and feedback, and on whether DRN inhibition is evidence for Dilp2 delivery. E remains the most defensible formal conclusion given explicit confounds and the prompt’s allowance for DRN Dilp2-independent function; B is the plausible physiological model most colleagues invoke but it requires assuming retrograde pool is protected from extracellular sink and that feedback does not invalidate glial experiment. No new data in round 1 resolves the confounds.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core facts remain: feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs; Dilp2 is secreted to hemolymph and also retrogradely transported via direct innervation to DRNs; Dilp2 drives NSC exit from quiescence; Dilp2 mutant blocks exit; Dilp2 freely crosses BBB; Imp-L2 binds Dilp2 and also freely crosses BBB; fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent; glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression; DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation, but DRNs may have Dilp2-independent function; unfed brain incubated with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin reactivates NSCs ex vivo.

Interpretive confounds repeatedly raised and now reinforced:
* Imp-L2 BBB permeability means fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; Imp-L2 enters brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde transport to DRNs. Hence the fat-body block cannot be read as loss of hemolymph Dilp2 per se.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to reduce IPC Dilp2 expression. The phenotype can be secondary to reduced synthesis of both hemolymph and retrograde pools, and not a clean local sequestration read-out.
* DRN activity is required for timely reactivation, but prompt explicitly allows a Dilp2-independent DRN function, so DRN inhibition is not diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption/retrograde delivery.
* Ex vivo high-dose insulin shows NSC insulin-responsiveness in principle, but supraphysiological concentration bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation and does not identify physiological route.

Arguments for B / hemolymph-secreted Dilp2:
* Fat-body Imp-L2 extracellular sink removes circulating Dilp2; Dilp2 crosses BBB so circulating ligand can reach brain; retrogradely transported Dilp2 is largely intracellular in transit/at release site and thus largely protected from extracellular Imp-L2. Block of reactivation by systemic sink therefore implies extracellular circulating pool is necessary. Colleagues 13,14,2,5,8,9 make this case, with 13/14/8 emphasizing protected intracellular retrograde pool and feedback reduction of IPC expression as consistent with loss of central signaling supplied by circulation.

Arguments for E / indeterminate:
* Majority colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,3,4,6,7 argue manipulations cannot cleanly dissociate hemolymph-secreted vs retrogradely transported pools because Imp-L2 crosses BBB and glial Imp-L2 feeds back on IPC expression. No BBB-impermeant sink, no retrograde-specific block with intact secretion, etc., is provided. Fat-body and glial sinks both remove central Dilp2 regardless of origin; glial sink additionally lowers source expression.

Argument for D / both:
* Colleague 8 claims fat-body soak shows circulating requirement and glial soak + DRN inhibition show neuronal/retrograde requirement.

Unresolved questions that keep the issue open:
* Is retrogradely transported Dilp2 extracellularly accessible to Imp-L2 after release in DRNs, or is it protected?
* How much of the glial Imp-L2 phenotype is acute sequestration vs secondary feedback down-regulation of IPC Dilp2 synthesis?
* Is DRN activity downstream of Dilp2 signaling or parallel/Dilp2-independent?

Current synthesis: Formally the data as given are confounded by free BBB permeability of both Dilp2 and Imp-L2 and by feedback down-regulation of IPC Dilp2 by central sequestration, so a clean assignment to A only, B only, both, or neither cannot be made. The majority reading in the deliberation is indeterminacy, E. A plausible but assumption-laden reading is that the extracellular sink experiments implicate circulating, BBB-crossing Dilp2 as the physiological driver, with retrograde delivery being modulatory rather than required, but that reading relies on the assumption that the retrograde pool is inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2 and that feedback effects are secondary rather than confounding.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The central question is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo requires Dilp2 that reaches the brain as circulating hemolymph hormone that crosses the BBB, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, both, or is not resolvable.

Evidence repeatedly cited:
* Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, free to cross BBB, and also transported retrogradely to DRNs.
* Dilp2 mutants fail to exit quiescence on feeding; high non-physiological bovine insulin incubation of an unfed brain can drive reactivation in vitro.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 and NSCs stay quiescent despite feeding.
* Imp-L2 itself freely crosses BBB.
* Glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation but concomitantly reduces Dilp2 expression in IPCs.
* DRN activity inhibition by potassium channel delays reactivation, but DRNs are explicitly allowed a Dilp2-independent function.

Arguments for B – hemolymph secreted Dilp2:
Fat-body Imp-L2 is a systemic extracellular sink. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit / synaptic; an extracellular binding protein should have limited access to a protected intracellular retrograde pool. That a systemic sink abolishes reactivation suggests the required pool is extracellular / circulating, and Dilp2 crossing BBB makes hemolymph-derived ligand accessible to brain. Glial Imp-L2 effect and IPC expression drop is read as feedback loss of central Dilp2 signaling supplied by circulating ligand. DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream of/parallel to systemic Dilp2.

Arguments for E – indeterminate:
Imp-L2 crosses BBB, so fat-body Imp-L2 is not hemolymph-specific; Imp-L2 enters brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that has crossed BBB from hemolymph or Dilp2 delivered retrogradely to DRNs. Block of reactivation can be loss of hemolymph Dilp2, loss of central Dilp2, or both.
Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and lowers IPC Dilp2 expression, a feedback confound that reduces both hemolymph and retrograde pools together. With BBB permeability of Dilp2, glial Imp-L2 also mops up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain.
DRN inhibition shows DRN output is needed but by stipulation DRN function may be Dilp2-independent, so inhibition is not diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption/retrograde delivery.
Ex vivo high insulin shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness but is supraphysiological and bypasses route/compartment constraints.

Group split in current round: majority Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,3,4,6,7 argue E – not possible to determine – because BBB permeability of Dilp2 and Imp-L2 and the feedback reduction of IPC Dilp2 expression make systemic vs retrograde pools inseparable. Minority Colleagues 2,5,8,9 argue B – hemolymph secreted Dilp2 is functionally required, reading fat-body sequestration as decisive and Imp-L2 BBB crossing as reinforcing a humoral model. One colleague earlier argued D both pools required.

Unresolved points that remain:
* Would a protected intracellular retrograde Dilp2 pool be truly inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2 that has entered brain? No manipulation specifically tests intracellular vs extracellular accessibility.
* Is glial Imp-L2 induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression a primary cause of NSC quiescence or a secondary consequence of lost central Dilp2 signaling?
* Is DRN activity requirement downstream of Dilp2 signaling or Dilp2-independent, and does that matter for source attribution?
* No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph Dilp2, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport is presented.

Current best assessment remains indeterminate on the data as given: the experiments cannot cleanly dissociate hemolymph-derived BBB-crossing Dilp2 from retrogradely transported IPC→DRN Dilp2, and DRN requirement is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core issue is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo requires Dilp2 that is secreted into hemolymph and crosses the BBB, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, both, or neither, given that Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, is secreted to hemolymph, is also retrogradely transported to DRNs, Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB, and DRNs are explicitly allowed a Dilp2-independent function.

Held facts:
- Dilp2 mutant fails to reactivate on feeding.
- Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
- DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation.
- Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

Arguments for E / not possible to determine, dominant in round 1:
* Imp-L2 crosses BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 therefore is not a hemolymph-only sink; it also delivers functional Imp-L2 into brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. The block cannot be read as hemolymph-specific.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. The phenotype can be secondary to reduced source synthesis, reducing both hemolymph and retrograde pools together, and the manipulation is intra-cerebral so the two pools remain inseparable.
* DRN inhibition shows DRN activity is required but, by prompt, DRNs may act Dilp2-independently, so inhibition is non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption in DRNs.
* Bovine insulin rescue shows insulin signalling is sufficient in principle but uses very high non-physiological concentration and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation; it does not identify physiological route.

Arguments for B / hemolymph-secreted, minority but refined:
* Extracellular sink logic: Imp-L2 acts extracellularly. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit/at delivery and largely protected from an extracellular binding protein until released. Fat-body systemic sink abolishes reactivation, therefore the accessible extracellular, circulating pool is required and a protected retrograde-only pool would be insufficient.
* Imp-L2 crossing BBB strengthens humoral reading: removing circulating Dilp2 also removes the extracellular Dilp2 in brain after BBB crossing; loss of central signalling explains feedback reduction of IPC Dilp2.
* Glial Imp-L2 is interpreted as sequestration of Dilp2 that has entered brain from circulation, with IPC down-regulation as downstream feedback, not a confound.
* DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream of/parallel to systemic Dilp2.

Disagreements noted:
- Clean interpretability of fat-body Imp-L2: E camp stresses BBB permeability makes it non-compartmentalised; B camp treats BBB permeability as expected for a circulating ligand model and argues intracellular retrograde pool would be sink-protected.
- Role of glial Imp-L2 feedback: E camp says feedback on IPC expression makes experiment ambiguous; B camp says feedback is predicted by loss of central signalling supplied by circulation.
- Diagnostic value of DRN inhibition: all agree DRN activity required, disagreement on whether this implicates retrograde Dilp2 uptake given explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function.

Unresolved:
- Is there any manipulation that isolates retrograde intracellular Dilp2 from extracellular hemolymph-derived Dilp2 in brain? No BBB-impermeant sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport is presented.
- Would a protected intracellular retrograde pool remain functional in presence of extracellular Imp-L2? In principle yes, but if retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN microenvironment it could still be accessible to Imp-L2 that crosses BBB. The data do not resolve accessibility.

Current synthesis: Confounds of free BBB permeability for both Dilp2 and Imp-L2, glial Imp-L2 feedback on IPC Dilp2 synthesis, and explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function prevent clean dissociation of hemolymph-derived BBB-crossing Dilp2 vs retrogradely delivered DRN Dilp2. The data show central Dilp2 signalling is necessary and hemolymph Dilp2 is formally plausible, and the B camp’s intracellular-protection argument is mechanistically plausible, but on the information as given the physiological source cannot be assigned to A, B, both, or neither with certainty. Majority colleagues remain on E, and my own assessment stays indeterminate.

reflection_text.1:
The core facts remain: Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, also retrogradely transported to DRNs, Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross BBB, Dilp2 mutant blocks exit from quiescence, fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent, glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation but DRNs may have a Dilp2-independent function, ex vivo very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation.

Two interpretive camps persist.

B camp: fat-body Imp-L2 is the decisive systemic necessity test. Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein; retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit / largely synaptic-private, so an extracellular sink should not neutralize it. The fact that a systemic extracellular sink abolishes feeding-induced reactivation therefore shows an extracellular accessible pool is required. Dilp2 crosses BBB so hemolymph-derived ligand can reach brain. Imp-L2 crossing BBB reinforces this: the sink removes Dilp2 from hemolymph and from the brain extracellular space that is fed by circulation. Glial Imp-L2 blocking reactivation and lowering IPC Dilp2 expression is read as loss of central Dilp2 signaling supplied from circulation feeding back to IPC output, not a separate retrograde requirement. DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2, explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent. In vitro high insulin shows ligand sufficiency for brain tissue.

E camp: Imp-L2 freely crosses BBB, so fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; it also delivers Imp-L2 into brain where it can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. The block is therefore compatible with loss of hemolymph, central, or both pools. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, so the phenotype can be secondary to feedback down-regulation of the source, lowering both hemolymph-secreted and retrograde pools together. With Dilp2 BBB-permeable, glial sequestration will also mop up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain. DRN inhibition is not diagnostic because DRNs may function independently of Dilp2 absorption. Ex vivo high insulin is supraphysiological bypass, shows sufficiency in principle not physiological route.

Unresolved issues: whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 is truly inaccessible to an extracellular Imp-L2 sink once released at DRN terminals; the causal direction of glial Imp-L2 → reduced IPC Dilp2 expression vs reduced IPC expression → NSC phenotype; whether free BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes any peripheral sink inherently central; no manipulation isolates hemolymph Dilp2 while sparing retrograde delivery, nor BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, nor IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport.

Disagreements centre on interpretability of Imp-L2 manipulations given BBB permeability and feedback, and on whether DRN inhibition is evidence for Dilp2 delivery. E remains the most defensible formal conclusion given explicit confounds and the prompt’s allowance for DRN Dilp2-independent function; B is the plausible physiological model most colleagues invoke but it requires assuming retrograde pool is protected from extracellular sink and that feedback does not invalidate glial experiment. No new data in round 1 resolves the confounds.
reflection_text.4:

* Imp-L2 BBB permeability means fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; Imp-L2 enters brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde transport to DRNs. Hence the fat-body block cannot be read as loss of hemolymph Dilp2 per se.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but also feeds back to reduce IPC Dilp2 expression. The phenotype can be secondary to reduced synthesis of both hemolymph and retrograde pools, and not a clean local sequestration read-out.
* DRN activity is required for timely reactivation, but prompt explicitly allows a Dilp2-independent DRN function, so DRN inhibition is not diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption/retrograde delivery.

* Fat-body Imp-L2 extracellular sink removes circulating Dilp2; Dilp2 crosses BBB so circulating ligand can reach brain; retrogradely transported Dilp2 is largely intracellular in transit/at release site and thus largely protected from extracellular Imp-L2. Block of reactivation by systemic sink therefore implies extracellular circulating pool is necessary. * Majority colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,3,4,6,7 argue manipulations cannot cleanly dissociate hemolymph-secreted vs retrogradely transported pools because Imp-L2 crosses BBB and glial Imp-L2 feeds back on IPC expression. Unresolved:
- Whether retrogradely delivered Dilp2 is ever extracellularly accessible to Imp-L2 after release, and whether DRN-local release would be protected.
- Whether glial Imp-L2-induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression is causal for the NSC block or a secondary feedback readout.
- Whether DRN activity requirement can be used at all to infer Dilp2 dependence given explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent function.

Current belief: The confounds around BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein, the feedback down-regulation of IPC Dilp2 by glial Imp-L2, and the explicitly non-diagnostic DRN manipulation mean the data as presented do not allow clean separation of hemolymph-secreted BBB-crossing Dilp2 vs IPC→DRN retrograde Dilp2. The formal answer is therefore E, not possible to determine. The parsimonious humoral reading is widely made in the literature, but it is not forced by the information given alone.
reflection_text.15:
The core question remains whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo is driven by Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and reaching the brain by free BBB crossing, by Dilp2 retrogradely transported from IPCs to DRNs, by both, or is indeterminate. The evidence repeatedly cited is: Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph and also retrogradely transported to DRNs; Dilp2 mutant blocks exit from quiescence; Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB; fat body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 and blocks reactivation; glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression; DRN activity inhibition delays reactivation but DRNs may act independently of Dilp2 absorption; very high non-physiological bovine insulin rescues an unfed brain ex vivo.

The confounds that persist after round 1 are still dominating the current round:

* BBB permeability makes the sinks non-compartmentalised. Imp-L2 crosses the BBB, so fat body Imp-L2 is both a hemolymph sink and a central extracellular sink. It can sequester Dilp2 already inside the CNS whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery/release in DRNs. E camp stresses this makes fat body loss of reactivation compatible with loss of hemolymph, central, or both pools.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but concomitantly lowers IPC Dilp2 expression, i.e. a brain-to-IPC feedback that reduces both hemolymph-secreted and retrograde pools together. That makes the glial experiment an ambiguous read-out of local sequestration vs secondary reduction of source output.
* DRN inhibition is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent, so DRN requirement does not demonstrate a requirement for Dilp2 uptake/absorption by DRNs, nor for retrograde delivery.
* The ex vivo high insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness but is supraphysiological and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation.

B camp colleagues 2,5,8,9,13,14 argue the extracellular sink logic is decisive: an extracellular binding protein should not access an intracellular/neurally compartmentalised retrograde pool, so abolition of reactivation by fat body Imp-L2 implies a requirement for extracellular accessible, circulating Dilp2 that crosses the BBB. They read glial Imp-L2-induced reduction in IPC Dilp2 as expected feedback loss of central signalling supplied by hemolymph-derived Dilp2, and read DRN inhibition as downstream of systemic signalling.

E camp colleagues 1,3,4,6,7,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 counter that Imp-L2 in the brain will bind Dilp2 released extracellularly from DRN terminals, and Dilp2 freely equilibrates across BBB, so pools cannot be separated. The intracellular protection argument for the retrograde pool is not established by the information given, and the feedback reduction of IPC expression means glial sequestration cannot be used to isolate a central pool. No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph Dilp2, or secretion-only block sparing retrograde transport is presented.

The current round is still split, with a clear majority ~E and a minority ~B, no D now. The unresolved issues that remain important are: anatomical accessibility of retrogradedly delivered Dilp2 to extracellular Imp-L2; whether the observed IPC expression down-regulation after glial Imp-L2 is primary feedback or a confound; and whether free BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes any systemic manipulation intrinsically central. On the information as given the hemolymph vs retrograde pools cannot be cleanly dissociated, and a definitive assignment to A, B, both or neither is not justified.

reflection_text.16:
The core issue is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo requires Dilp2 that is secreted into hemolymph and crosses the BBB, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, both, or neither, given that Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, is secreted to hemolymph, is also retrogradely transported to DRNs, Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB, and DRNs are explicitly allowed a Dilp2-independent function.

Held facts:
- Dilp2 mutant fails to reactivate on feeding.
- Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
- DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation.
- Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

Arguments for E / not possible to determine, dominant in round 1:
* Imp-L2 crosses BBB. Fat-body Imp-L2 therefore is not a hemolymph-only sink; it also delivers functional Imp-L2 into brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether that Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. The block cannot be read as hemolymph-specific.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. The phenotype can be secondary to reduced source synthesis, reducing both hemolymph and retrograde pools together, and the manipulation is intra-cerebral so the two pools remain inseparable.
* DRN inhibition shows DRN activity is required but, by prompt, DRNs may act Dilp2-independently, so inhibition is non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption in DRNs.
* Bovine insulin rescue shows insulin signalling is sufficient in principle but uses very high non-physiological concentration and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation; it does not identify physiological route.

Arguments for B / hemolymph-secreted, minority but refined:
* Extracellular sink logic: Imp-L2 acts extracellularly. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit/at delivery and largely protected from an extracellular binding protein until released. Fat-body systemic sink abolishes reactivation, therefore the accessible extracellular, circulating pool is required and a protected retrograde-only pool would be insufficient.
* Imp-L2 crossing BBB strengthens humoral reading: removing circulating Dilp2 also removes the extracellular Dilp2 in brain after BBB crossing; loss of central signalling explains feedback reduction of IPC Dilp2.
* Glial Imp-L2 is interpreted as sequestration of Dilp2 that has entered brain from circulation, with IPC down-regulation as downstream feedback, not a confound.
* DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream of/parallel to systemic Dilp2.

Disagreements noted:
- Clean interpretability of fat-body Imp-L2: E camp stresses BBB permeability makes it non-compartmentalised; B camp treats BBB permeability as expected for a circulating ligand model and argues intracellular retrograde pool would be sink-protected.
- Role of glial Imp-L2 feedback: E camp says feedback on IPC expression makes experiment ambiguous; B camp says feedback is predicted by loss of central signalling supplied by circulation.
- Diagnostic value of DRN inhibition: all agree DRN activity required, disagreement on whether this implicates retrograde Dilp2 uptake given explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function.

Unresolved:
- Is there any manipulation that isolates retrograde intracellular Dilp2 from extracellular hemolymph-derived Dilp2 in brain? No BBB-impermeant sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport is presented.
- Would a protected intracellular retrograde pool remain functional in presence of extracellular Imp-L2? In principle yes, but if retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN microenvironment it could still be accessible to Imp-L2 that crosses BBB. The data do not resolve accessibility.

Current synthesis: Confounds of free BBB permeability for both Dilp2 and Imp-L2, glial Imp-L2 feedback on IPC Dilp2 synthesis, and explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function prevent clean dissociation of hemolymph-derived BBB-crossing Dilp2 vs retrogradely delivered DRN Dilp2. The data show central Dilp2 signalling is necessary and hemolymph Dilp2 is formally plausible, and the B camp’s intracellular-protection argument is mechanistically plausible, but on the information as given the physiological source cannot be assigned to A, B, both, or neither with certainty. Majority colleagues remain on E, and my own assessment stays indeterminate.

7.text:
E. Not possible to determine based on the information provided

Dilp2 is necessary for feeding-induced NSC exit from quiescence and it can reach the brain by two formally distinct routes: secretion into the hemolymph with free BBB crossing, and retrograde neuronal delivery from IPCs to DRNs. The manipulations as described do not cleanly dissociate those two pools.

* Fat-body Imp-L2. Imp-L2 expressed in the fat body soaks hemolymph Dilp2 and blocks reactivation. Imp-L2 itself freely crosses the BBB, so fat-body derived Imp-L2 is also present in the brain parenchyma where it can sequester Dilp2 already inside the CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB from the hemolymph or Dilp2 that has been delivered to DRNs by retrograde transport. The block is therefore compatible with loss of hemolymph Dilp2, loss of central Dilp2, or loss of both.

* Glial Imp-L2. Glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation but it concomitantly reduces Dilp2 expression in the IPCs. The NSC phenotype can therefore be read as a primary central sequestration effect and/or as a secondary consequence of feedback down-regulation of IPC Dilp2 synthesis, which reduces both the hemolymph secreted pool and the retrograde neuronal pool together. Because Dilp2 is BBB permeable, glial Imp-L2 will also mop up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered the brain.

* DRN manipulation. Inhibition of DRN activity by a potassium channel delays reactivation, but DRNs are explicitly allowed to have a Dilp2-independent function. DRN requirement therefore establishes a requirement for DRN output for timely reactivation, not a requirement for Dilp2 uptake/absorption by DRNs.

* Ex vivo rescue. Incubation of an unfed brain with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation. This shows NSCs are insulin responsive in principle, but it is a supraphysiological bypass that does not establish the physiological route, concentration or compartment used in vivo.

Because both Dilp2 and Imp-L2 freely cross the BBB, no manipulation isolates hemolymph Dilp2 from brain Dilp2. The central sequestration manipulation also feeds back on IPC synthesis. With those confounds the hemolymph-secreted, BBB-crossing pool and the retrogradely transported IPC→DRN pool cannot be separated on the data given, and a BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, a retrograde transport block that spares hemolymph Dilp2, or a secretion-only block that spares retrograde transport is not described. The physiological source therefore cannot be assigned to A, B, both or neither.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph

The feeding requirement is satisfied by an extracellular, circulating pool that can be removed by a systemic sink, and the manipulations are consistent with retrogradely transported Dilp2 being protected from that sink.

Fat body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein. It binds Dilp2 in the hemolymph and it also crosses the BBB, so it is present in the brain extracellular space. Dilp2 itself is free to cross the BBB, so the brain extracellular Dilp2 that is available to the NSC niche under normal feeding is the Dilp2 that has arrived from the circulation. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 from IPCs to DRNs is in transit intracellularly in axons and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment. An extracellular sink will have poor access to that intracellular/in-transit pool until and unless it is released into the extracellular space. If a protected retrograde pool were sufficient to drive reactivation, removal of the accessible circulating pool by a fat body sink should not abolish feeding-induced reactivation. The fact that fat body Imp-L2 keeps NSCs quiescent despite feeding and despite IPCs being able to make Dilp2 is exactly the signature of a requirement for an accessible circulating pool.

Imp-L2 crossing the BBB does not make the fat body manipulation non-specific, it reinforces the humoral model. The sink enters the brain and sequesters extracellular Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB from the hemolymph. That is the pool that is normally available to the parenchyma.

Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and lowers IPC Dilp2 expression. That is the feedback you expect if central Dilp2 signalling that normally maintains IPC output is supplied by circulating Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB and is now being sequestered centrally. Loss of brain Dilp2 signalling feeds back to down-regulate the source. It is not evidence that the manipulation is confounded for a retrograde versus humoral distinction; it is downstream feedback from loss of the systemic signal.

DRN inhibition delays reactivation but DRNs are explicitly allowed a Dilp2-independent function. DRN requirement is therefore a requirement for DRN output, not proof that Dilp2 must be retrogradely absorbed by DRNs to act. DRNs can act downstream of, or in parallel to, systemic Dilp2 signalling that reaches the brain after BBB crossing.

I’m leaning B, Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph, and I think the BBB permeability point actually supports rather than undermines that reading.

Yes Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both cross the BBB freely, but that does not make fat-body Imp-L2 non-specific for the accessible circulating pool. Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein. It will bind Dilp2 in the hemolymph and it will bind Dilp2 that is extracellular in the brain after it has crossed the BBB from the circulation. What it will not efficiently bind is Dilp2 that is in transit inside an IPC axon or that is tightly compartmentalised at a DRN terminal before release. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit and acts in a largely synaptic/private compartment. An extracellular sink is largely protected from that pool.

That functional inaccessibility matters for the fat-body experiment. Fat-body Imp-L2 makes a systemic extracellular sink. Removing the hemolymph Dilp2 pool also removes the pool of Dilp2 that can appear extracellularly in the brain after BBB crossing. It sequesters Dilp2 that is extracellular in the brain parenchyma, i.e. Dilp2 that has arrived from the hemolymph via free BBB crossing. The concomitant reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression is exactly the feedback you expect when brain Dilp2 signaling supplied by circulating ligand is acutely lost: loss of central sensing feeds back to down-regulate the source neurons. That feedback reduces both hemolymph secreted and retrograde pools together, which is why IPC expression drops, but the primary event is loss of signaling supplied by the circulation.

DRN requirement is therefore compatible with DRNs acting downstream of, or in parallel to, systemic Dilp2 that has reached the brain by BBB crossing. It does not demonstrate that Dilp2 must be retrogradely absorbed by DRNs to drive reactivation.

The ex vivo rescue with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin shows NSCs are intrinsically insulin responsive and that ligand access to brain tissue is sufficient to drive exit from quiescence. In vivo that access is provided by Dilp2 that is free to cross the BBB from the hemolymph after feeding.

The parsimonious physiological source in the intact feeding animal is Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and acting in the brain after BBB crossing. 16.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core question is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo requires Dilp2 that is secreted into hemolymph and crosses the BBB, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, both, or neither.

Held facts from prompt and rounds:
- Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, and also retrogradely transported to DRNs.
- Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB. Imp-L2 also freely crosses the BBB.
- Dilp2 mutant fails to reactivate on feeding.
- Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and also reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
- DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation; DRNs may have Dilp2-independent function.
- Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

Arguments for E / not possible to determine, now dominant in round 2:
* Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes fat-body Imp-L2 a systemic + central sink. It can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. Block cannot be read as hemolymph-specific.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. The NSC phenotype can be secondary to reduced source synthesis, reducing both hemolymph and retrograde pools together. The manipulation is intra-cerebral and therefore does not isolate retrograde vs humoral.
* DRN inhibition shows DRN activity is required but is explicitly non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption because DRNs may act Dilp2-independently.
* Ex vivo insulin rescue shows sufficiency of insulin signalling in principle but uses supra-physiological dose and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation.

Arguments for B / hemolymph-secreted, minority refined in round 2:
* Compartment access argument: Imp-L2 is extracellular. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit / largely synaptic/private. An extracellular sink should have limited access to a protected intracellular retrograde pool. Fat-body extracellular sink abolishes reactivation, therefore an accessible extracellular/circulating pool is required.
* BBB permeability of Imp-L2 strengthens humoral reading: any Dilp2 extracellular in brain after BBB crossing is derived from hemolymph. Imp-L2 entering brain mops up circulating-derived extracellular Dilp2.
* Glial Imp-L2 feedback reducing IPC Dilp2 is interpreted as expected feedback loss of central Dilp2 signalling normally supplied by circulating Dilp2 that crossed BBB, not a confound.
* DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2 signalling.

Arguments for D / both:
* Fat-body sink shows hemolymph requirement, glial sink + DRN inhibition show requirement for Dilp2 that is transported to/acts on DRNs. Few colleagues hold this; most say manipulations are confounded.

Disagreements noted:
- Clean interpretability of fat-body Imp-L2: E camp stresses BBB permeability makes it non-compartmentalised; B camp argues BBB permeability is expected for humoral model and intracellular retrograde pool would be sink-protected.
- Role of glial Imp-L2 feedback: E camp says feedback on IPC expression makes experiment ambiguous, reduces both pools; B camp says feedback is predicted downstream loss of systemic signalling.
- Accessibility of retrogradely delivered Dilp2 to extracellular Imp-L2 after release: unresolved. If retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN microenvironment, it could be accessible to Imp-L2 that crossed BBB.

Unresolved:
- No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph secretion, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport presented.
- No data on whether retrograde Dilp2 remains intracellular/protected or becomes extracellularly accessible.
- Whether the reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 is a primary confound or downstream feedback.

Current synthesis: The data show central Dilp2 signalling is necessary and hemolymph Dilp2 is formally plausible and mechanistically parsimonious given extracellular sink logic. However free BBB permeability of both Dilp2 and Imp-L2, glial Imp-L2 feedback on IPC synthesis, and explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function prevent clean dissociation of hemolymph-derived BBB-crossing Dilp2 vs retrogradely delivered DRN Dilp2. No manipulation isolates the two pools without a second effect. Majority colleagues remain on E, and my assessment stays indeterminate: the physiological source cannot be assigned to A, B, C or D on the information given.

No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph secretion, no secretion-only block sparing retrograde transport is provided. B camp, persistent minority, argues compartment accessibility. Imp-L2 is an extracellular binding protein. reflection_text.17:
The question is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo is driven by Dilp2 that is secreted into the hemolymph and crosses the BBB, by Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, or by both/neither. Core agreed facts remain:

* Feeding induces Dilp2 in IPCs. Dilp2 is secreted to hemolymph and also retrogradely transported to DRNs.
* Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB.
* Dilp2 mutants fail to exit quiescence on feeding.
* Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and concomitantly reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
* DRN hyperpolarisation delays reactivation, but DRNs may have a Dilp2-independent function.
* Ex vivo unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation.

Persisting confounds:

* BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes systemic vs central manipulations non-compartmentalised. Fat-body Imp-L2 also raises central Imp-L2 and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that arrived by BBB crossing or by retrograde delivery. Hence fat-body block alone does not uniquely implicate hemolymph Dilp2.
* Glial Imp-L2 is intra-cerebral but feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 synthesis. NSC phenotype could be secondary to reduced source output, affecting both hemolymph and retrograde pools together. With Dilp2 BBB permeable, glial sequestration also removes hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain.
* DRN inhibition is explicitly allowed to be Dilp2-independent, so DRN requirement is non-diagnostic for Dilp2 delivery to DRNs.
* Bovine insulin rescue uses supraphysiological concentration and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation; sufficiency in vitro does not identify physiological route in vivo.

Arguments for B, Dilp2 secreted to hemolymph, refined in round 2:
* Imp-L2 is an extracellular binding protein. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit and at the site of delivery largely protected from extracellular sink until release. If a protected retrograde pool were sufficient, an extracellular systemic sink should not abolish reactivation. Fat-body sink abolishes reactivation → requirement for extracellular accessible pool.
* BBB permeability of Imp-L2 reinforces humoral interpretation: any Dilp2 present extracellularly in brain after BBB crossing is derived from hemolymph. Sink entering brain neutralises that pool.
* Glial Imp-L2 block + IPC expression drop read as feedback loss of central signalling normally supplied by circulating Dilp2 crossing BBB, not as confound.
* DRN requirement can be downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2 reaching brain via BBB.

Arguments for E, not possible to determine:
* No data given on subcellular accessibility of retrogradely delivered Dilp2 to extracellular Imp-L2. If retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRNs, Imp-L2 can sequester it, so fat-body and glial sinks are not selective for humoral vs retrograde.
* Because Imp-L2 crosses BBB, fat-body sink is also a central sink. No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing secretion, no secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport is provided.
* Glial Imp-L2 feedback on IPC expression ambiguously ties central sequestration to reduced source output, making it impossible to separate acute local sequestration from reduced production of both pools.
* DRN inhibition is explicitly non-diagnostic.

Unresolved points for me:
* Subcellular availability of retrogradely transported Dilp2: protected intracellular vs extracellularly released. Information given does not state this.
* Causality of IPC Dilp2 reduction after glial Imp-L2: secondary consequence of loss of central signalling vs primary confound that invalidates local read-out.
* Whether feedback reduction means both pools are reduced together, rendering manipulations uninformative.

Current stance: formally indeterminate remains the most conservative reading given the stated BBB permeability of both Dilp2 and Imp-L2 and the feedback effect of glial Imp-L2 on IPC expression, and the explicit allowance of a Dilp2-independent DRN function. The B interpretation relies on an unstated assumption that retrogradely transported Dilp2 is inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein. That assumption is plausible but not established in the information provided. Hence E is the defensible position, with B as the commonly quoted but under-determined alternative.

reflection_text.16:
The core question is whether feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo requires Dilp2 that is secreted into hemolymph and crosses the BBB, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN, both, or neither.

Held facts from prompt and rounds:
- Dilp2 is made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, and also retrogradely transported to DRNs.
- Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB. Imp-L2 also freely crosses the BBB.
- Dilp2 mutant fails to reactivate on feeding.
- Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and also reduces IPC Dilp2 expression.
- DRN hyperpolarization delays reactivation; DRNs may have Dilp2-independent function.
- Unfed brain + very high non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation ex vivo.

Arguments for E / not possible to determine, now dominant in round 2:
* Imp-L2 BBB permeability makes fat-body Imp-L2 a systemic + central sink. It can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs. Block cannot be read as hemolymph-specific.
* Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression. The NSC phenotype can be secondary to reduced source synthesis, reducing both hemolymph and retrograde pools together. The manipulation is intra-cerebral and therefore does not isolate retrograde vs humoral.
* DRN inhibition shows DRN activity is required but is explicitly non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption because DRNs may act Dilp2-independently.
* Ex vivo insulin rescue shows sufficiency of insulin signalling in principle but uses supra-physiological dose and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation.

Arguments for B / hemolymph-secreted, minority refined in round 2:
* Compartment access argument: Imp-L2 is extracellular. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit / largely synaptic/private. An extracellular sink should have limited access to a protected intracellular retrograde pool. Fat-body extracellular sink abolishes reactivation, therefore an accessible extracellular/circulating pool is required.
* BBB permeability of Imp-L2 strengthens humoral reading: any Dilp2 extracellular in brain after BBB crossing is derived from hemolymph. Imp-L2 entering brain mops up circulating-derived extracellular Dilp2.
* Glial Imp-L2 feedback reducing IPC Dilp2 is interpreted as expected feedback loss of central Dilp2 signalling normally supplied by circulating Dilp2 that crossed BBB, not a confound.
* DRN requirement is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2 signalling.

Arguments for D / both:
* Fat-body sink shows hemolymph requirement, glial sink + DRN inhibition show requirement for Dilp2 that is transported to/acts on DRNs. Few colleagues hold this; most say manipulations are confounded.

Disagreements noted:
- Clean interpretability of fat-body Imp-L2: E camp stresses BBB permeability makes it non-compartmentalised; B camp argues BBB permeability is expected for humoral model and intracellular retrograde pool would be sink-protected.
- Role of glial Imp-L2 feedback: E camp says feedback on IPC expression makes experiment ambiguous, reduces both pools; B camp says feedback is predicted downstream loss of systemic signalling.
- Accessibility of retrogradely delivered Dilp2 to extracellular Imp-L2 after release: unresolved. If retrograde Dilp2 is released extracellularly in DRN microenvironment, it could be accessible to Imp-L2 that crossed BBB.

Unresolved:
- No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph secretion, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport presented.
- No data on whether retrograde Dilp2 remains intracellular/protected or becomes extracellularly accessible.
- Whether the reduction in IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 is a primary confound or downstream feedback.

Current synthesis: The data show central Dilp2 signalling is necessary and hemolymph Dilp2 is formally plausible and mechanistically parsimonious given extracellular sink logic. However free BBB permeability of both Dilp2 and Imp-L2, glial Imp-L2 feedback on IPC synthesis, and explicit allowance for Dilp2-independent DRN function prevent clean dissociation of hemolymph-derived BBB-crossing Dilp2 vs retrogradely delivered DRN Dilp2. No manipulation isolates the two pools without a second effect. Majority colleagues remain on E, and my assessment stays indeterminate: the physiological source cannot be assigned to A, B, C or D on the information given.

Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB, so hemolymph-derived Dilp2 and brain extracellular Dilp2 are in rapid equilibrium. Fat-body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular sink. It binds Dilp2 in the hemolymph and, because Imp-L2 itself crosses the BBB, it also binds extracellular Dilp2 that is already present in the brain after BBB crossing. That is exactly the humoral model: remove accessible circulating ligand and you remove the ligand that can appear extracellularly in the brain.

The retrograde IPC→DRN pool is different in compartment access. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 moves intracellularly in axons and is released in a largely synaptic/private compartment. An extracellular binding protein has very limited access to an intracellular in-transit pool until and unless it is released. If a protected intracellular retrograde pool were sufficient to drive feeding-induced NSC exit, a systemic extracellular sink made in the fat body should not be able to abolish reactivation despite feeding and despite IPCs being able to make Dilp2. 1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core facts are unchanged: Dilp2 is feeding-induced in IPCs, secreted to hemolymph, also retrogradely transported to DRNs; Dilp2 drives NSC reactivation from quiescence; Dilp2 mutant blocks exit; Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB; fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent; glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression; DRN hyperpolarisation delays reactivation but DRNs may be Dilp2-independent; very high non-physiological bovine insulin ex vivo drives reactivation.

Interpretive split remains B vs E, with a minority D.

B camp, now sharpened with compartment-access reasoning: Imp-L2 is extracellular, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN is moved intracellularly in axons and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment, largely inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein until release. Fat-body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular sink that binds Dilp2 in hemolymph and, because Imp-L2 crosses BBB, also binds extracellular Dilp2 in brain after BBB crossing. Because Dilp2 also freely crosses BBB, brain extracellular Dilp2 is in rapid equilibrium with hemolymph-derived Dilp2. Therefore abolition of feeding-induced reactivation by a systemic extracellular sink is evidence for requirement for an extracellular-accessible, circulating pool. Imp-L2 crossing BBB is not a confound but reinforces humoral reading: it ensures Dilp2 that has already crossed is neutralised. Glial Imp-L2 is an intra-cerebral extracellular sink: it blocks reactivation and feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression, read as loss of central signalling supplied by circulating ligand feeding back to source. DRN inhibition is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2, explicitly allowed Dilp2-independent. Ex vivo high insulin shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness.

E camp: Imp-L2 freely crosses BBB, so fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; Imp-L2 enters brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that has arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs and is extracellularly accessible after release. Block is therefore compatible with loss of hemolymph, central, or both pools. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but concomitantly reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, so phenotype can be secondary to feedback down-regulation of source, lowering both hemolymph-secreted and retrograde pools together. With Dilp2 BBB-permeable, glial sequestration also mops up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic because DRNs may function independently of Dilp2 absorption. Ex vivo supraphysiological insulin is bypass, shows sufficiency not physiological route. No manipulation isolates hemolymph Dilp2 while sparing retrograde delivery, nor BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, nor IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport.

Unresolved issues that keep formal indeterminacy: whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 is truly inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2 once released at DRN terminals; causal direction of glial Imp-L2 → reduced IPC Dilp2 expression vs reduced expression → NSC phenotype; whether free BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes any peripheral sink inherently central; no data on synaptic accessibility of retrograde pool. Disagreements centre on interpretability of Imp-L2 manipulations given BBB permeability and feedback, and on whether compartment-access protection argument justifies B.

I retain E as the most defensible formal conclusion given the information as stated — the data do not allow clean dissociation of A vs B, and the prompt explicitly allows DRN Dilp2-independent function. B remains the plausible physiological reading most colleagues invoke if one assumes retrograde pool is protected from extracellular sink and feedback does not invalidate glial experiment. No new data in round 3 resolves confounds; arguments reiterated.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is which physiologic Dilp2 pool drives feeding-induced NSC reactivation in vivo: retrogradely transported IPC→DRN Dilp2, hemolymph secreted Dilp2 that crosses BBB, both, or indeterminate.

Stable facts:
- Dilp2 made in IPCs on feeding, secreted to hemolymph, free to cross BBB.
- Dilp2 also transported by direct innervation/retrograde transport to DRNs.
- Dilp2 mutant fails to exit quiescence on feeding.
- Imp-L2 is a Dilp2 binding protein that freely crosses BBB.
- Fat body Imp-L2 overexpression soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSCs stay quiescent, fail to reactivate.
- Glial Imp-L2 overexpression also blocks reactivation and lowers IPC Dilp2 expression.
- DRN activity inhibition by potassium channel delays reactivation, but DRNs may have Dilp2-independent function.
- Unfed brain incubated with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation.

Arguments for B – hemolymph secreted:
- Fat body Imp-L2 is an extracellular systemic sink. Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both cross BBB, so hemolymph-derived Dilp2 equilibrates with brain extracellular space. Removal of accessible circulating Dilp2 blocks reactivation.
- Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is intracellular in transit and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment, largely inaccessible to extracellular binding protein. If protected retrograde pool were sufficient, extracellular sink should not abolish reactivation. Block read as requirement for accessible circulating pool.
- Imp-L2 crossing BBB strengthens humoral reading: Imp-L2 enters brain and sequesters Dilp2 already crossed from circulation. Glial Imp-L2 block + reduced IPC expression interpreted as feedback loss of central Dilp2 signalling normally supplied by circulating Dilp2 crossing BBB.
- DRN requirement compatible with DRNs acting downstream of systemic Dilp2, given allowed Dilp2-independent DRN function.
- Ex vivo insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness, consistent with circulating ligand reaching brain.

Arguments for E – not possible to determine:
- Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross BBB. Fat body Imp-L2 therefore also raises brain Imp-L2 and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing or retrograde transport. Fat body sink is not hemolymph-specific.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and feeds back to reduce IPC Dilp2 synthesis, so NSC block can be secondary to reduced production of both hemolymph and retrograde pools, not clean local sequestration readout.
- DRN inhibition shows requirement for DRN activity but not for Dilp2 uptake by DRNs, explicitly allowed to be Dilp2 independent.
- Ex vivo insulin rescue uses supraphysiological concentration and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation.
- No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block sparing hemolymph Dilp2, no IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport.

Current round distribution:
Majority 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,3,4,6,7,18 maintain E. Minority 13,14,2,5,8,9 maintain B with extracellular-access vs intracellular-protected retrograde argument. Colleague 8 moved from previous D both A and B to B in this round; Colleague 18 moved from previous B to E.

Unresolved questions persisting:
- Is retrogradely delivered Dilp2 extracellularly accessible to Imp-L2 at DRN terminals, or protected intracellular/synaptic?
- Is reduced IPC Dilp2 expression after glial Imp-L2 cause or consequence of NSC block/feedback?
- Can any manipulation with given tools uniquely isolate hemolymph-secreted from retrogradely transported Dilp2 given free BBB permeability of ligand and binding protein?

Current understanding remains that data are formally compatible with hemolymph-only, retrograde-only, both, or neither, and majority reading is that manipulations are confounded by free BBB permeability and feedback on IPC synthesis, so physiological source cannot be assigned. Persistent minority reading treats extracellular sink inaccessibility to intracellular retrograde pool as sufficient to implicate hemolymph-secreted Dilp2 as required source.

reflection_text.1:
The core facts are unchanged: Dilp2 is feeding-induced in IPCs, secreted to hemolymph, also retrogradely transported to DRNs; Dilp2 drives NSC reactivation from quiescence; Dilp2 mutant blocks exit; Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross the BBB; fat-body Imp-L2 soaks hemolymph Dilp2 → NSC stay quiescent; glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation and reduces IPC Dilp2 expression; DRN hyperpolarisation delays reactivation but DRNs may be Dilp2-independent; very high non-physiological bovine insulin ex vivo drives reactivation.

Interpretive split remains B vs E, with a minority D.

B camp, now sharpened with compartment-access reasoning: Imp-L2 is extracellular, Dilp2 that is retrogradely transported IPC→DRN is moved intracellularly in axons and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment, largely inaccessible to an extracellular binding protein until release. Fat-body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular sink that binds Dilp2 in hemolymph and, because Imp-L2 crosses BBB, also binds extracellular Dilp2 in brain after BBB crossing. Because Dilp2 also freely crosses BBB, brain extracellular Dilp2 is in rapid equilibrium with hemolymph-derived Dilp2. Therefore abolition of feeding-induced reactivation by a systemic extracellular sink is evidence for requirement for an extracellular-accessible, circulating pool. Imp-L2 crossing BBB is not a confound but reinforces humoral reading: it ensures Dilp2 that has already crossed is neutralised. Glial Imp-L2 is an intra-cerebral extracellular sink: it blocks reactivation and feeds back to lower IPC Dilp2 expression, read as loss of central signalling supplied by circulating ligand feeding back to source. DRN inhibition is compatible with DRNs acting downstream/parallel to systemic Dilp2, explicitly allowed Dilp2-independent. Ex vivo high insulin shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness.

E camp: Imp-L2 freely crosses BBB, so fat-body overexpression is not hemolymph-specific; Imp-L2 enters brain and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that has arrived by BBB crossing from hemolymph or by retrograde delivery to DRNs and is extracellularly accessible after release. Block is therefore compatible with loss of hemolymph, central, or both pools. Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation but concomitantly reduces IPC Dilp2 expression, so phenotype can be secondary to feedback down-regulation of source, lowering both hemolymph-secreted and retrograde pools together. With Dilp2 BBB-permeable, glial sequestration also mops up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered brain. DRN inhibition is non-diagnostic because DRNs may function independently of Dilp2 absorption. Ex vivo supraphysiological insulin is bypass, shows sufficiency not physiological route. No manipulation isolates hemolymph Dilp2 while sparing retrograde delivery, nor BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, nor IPC secretion-specific block sparing retrograde transport.

Unresolved issues that keep formal indeterminacy: whether retrogradely transported Dilp2 is truly inaccessible to extracellular Imp-L2 once released at DRN terminals; causal direction of glial Imp-L2 → reduced IPC Dilp2 expression vs reduced expression → NSC phenotype; whether free BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein makes any peripheral sink inherently central; no data on synaptic accessibility of retrograde pool. Disagreements centre on interpretability of Imp-L2 manipulations given BBB permeability and feedback, and on whether compartment-access protection argument justifies B.

I retain E as the most defensible formal conclusion given the information as stated — the data do not allow clean dissociation of A vs B, and the prompt explicitly allows DRN Dilp2-independent function. B remains the plausible physiological reading most colleagues invoke if one assumes retrograde pool is protected from extracellular sink and feedback does not invalidate glial experiment. No new data in round 3 resolves confounds; arguments reiterated.
reflection_text.12:

- Fat body Imp-L2 is an extracellular systemic sink. Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both cross BBB, so hemolymph-derived Dilp2 equilibrates with brain extracellular space. Removal of accessible circulating Dilp2 blocks reactivation.

- Ex vivo insulin rescue shows intrinsic insulin responsiveness, consistent with circulating ligand reaching brain.

- Dilp2 and Imp-L2 both freely cross BBB. Fat body Imp-L2 therefore also raises brain Imp-L2 and can sequester Dilp2 already inside CNS, whether Dilp2 arrived by BBB crossing or retrograde transport. Fat body sink is not hemolymph-specific.
- Glial Imp-L2 blocks reactivation and feeds back to reduce IPC Dilp2 synthesis, so NSC block can be secondary to reduced production of both hemolymph and retrograde pools, not clean local sequestration readout.

- Ex vivo insulin rescue uses supraphysiological concentration and bypasses normal transport/compartmentalisation.

Current understanding remains that data are formally compatible with hemolymph-only, retrograde-only, both, or neither, and majority reading is that manipulations are confounded by free BBB permeability and feedback on IPC synthesis, so physiological source cannot be assigned. 2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph

I think the fat-body Imp-L2 sink is the cleanest in vivo necessity test we have, and the BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein actually sharpens rather than blurs the humoral reading.

Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB and Imp-L2 is free to cross the BBB. That means Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and Dilp2 present extracellularly in the brain parenchyma are in rapid equilibrium. Fat-body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein. It binds Dilp2 in the hemolymph, and because it itself crosses the BBB it also binds Dilp2 that is already extracellular in the brain after it has arrived from the circulation. That is exactly the signature of a humoral supply: an extracellular sink present both systemically and centrally removes the circulating-derived brain extracellular pool.

Compartment access is what distinguishes the hemolymph pool from the retrograde IPC → DRN pool for this manipulation. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is moved intracellularly in axons and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment. Until release it is in transit intracellularly and functionally protected from an extracellular binding protein. An extracellular sink has very limited access to an in-transit intracellular pool.

If a protected intracellular retrograde pool were sufficient to drive feeding-induced NSC exit, removal of the accessible extracellular circulating pool by a fat-body sink should not be sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent despite feeding and despite IPCs being feeding induced. The fact that fat-body Imp-L2 soaking hemolymph Dilp2 blocks reactivation is most naturally read as a requirement for an extracellular-accessible pool, i.e. Dilp2 that reaches the brain from the circulation.

Imp-L2 crossing the BBB does not make the fat-body manipulation non-specific. Any Dilp2 that is extracellular in the brain after free BBB crossing is derived from the hemolymph. Imp-L2 entering the brain simply ensures that Dilp2 that has already crossed is also neutralised. That is the humoral model.

Glial Imp-L2 fits the same logic. Glial Imp-L2 is an intra-cerebral extracellular sink. It blocks reactivation and concomitantly reduces Dilp2 expression in IPCs. That is the feedback you expect if central Dilp2 signalling that normally sustains IPC output is supplied by circulating Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB: acute loss of brain extracellular Dilp2 signalling feeds back to down-regulate the source neurons, secondarily lowering both the secreted and the retrograde pools. The reduction in IPC expression is downstream of loss of systemic/central signalling, not a confound that erases the local read-out.

DRN inhibition delays reactivation, but the prompt explicitly allows DRNs a Dilp2-independent function. A DRN requirement therefore establishes a need for DRN output for timely reactivation, not that Dilp2 must be retrogradely absorbed by DRNs to drive reactivation. DRNs can act downstream of, or in parallel to, systemic Dilp2 that has reached the brain by free BBB crossing.

The ex vivo rescue with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin shows NSCs are intrinsically insulin responsive and that direct ligand access to brain tissue is sufficient in principle. In vivo that access under feeding is provided by Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and free to cross the BBB.

Removal of accessible circulating Dilp2 by a systemic extracellular sink that also enters the brain blocks feeding-induced reactivation, and direct brain ligand exposure is sufficient to drive it. Retrograde IPC→DRN delivery can occur, but the sink experiments show the extracellular circulating pool is the one that is required in the intact animal. The parsimonious physiological source in the fed animal is Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph from IPCs and acting in the brain after BBB crossing.

3.text:
E. Not possible to determine based on the information provided

Dilp2 is necessary for feeding-induced NSC exit from quiescence and on the facts given it can reach the NSC compartment by two formally distinct routes that are not dissociated by the manipulations described: i) secretion into the hemolymph with free BBB crossing, and ii) retrograde neuronal delivery IPC → DRN.

* Fat-body Imp-L2. Fat-body Imp-L2 soaks Dilp2 in the hemolymph and blocks reactivation. Both Dilp2 and Imp-L2 freely cross the BBB. Fat-body derived Imp-L2 is therefore present in the brain parenchyma where it can sequester Dilp2 already inside the CNS, i.e. Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB from the hemolymph and Dilp2 that has been retrogradely delivered to DRNs and is extracellularly accessible after release. The block is compatible with loss of a hemolymph pool, loss of a central pool, or loss of both.

* Glial Imp-L2. Glial Imp-L2 also blocks reactivation but it concomitantly reduces Dilp2 expression in the IPCs. The NSC phenotype can therefore be read as acute central sequestration and/or as a secondary consequence of brain-to-IPC feedback down-regulation of the source neurons, which lowers both the hemolymph-secreted pool and the retrogradely transported pool together. Because Dilp2 is BBB permeable, glial sequestration will also mop up hemolymph-derived Dilp2 that has entered the brain, so no clean local vs systemic read-out is obtained.

* DRN requirement. Inhibition of DRN activity by a potassium channel delays reactivation, but the prompt explicitly allows DRNs to have a Dilp2-independent function in NSC reactivation. DRN dependence therefore establishes a requirement for DRN output for timely reactivation, not a requirement for Dilp2 uptake by DRNs or for retrogradely transported Dilp2 as the physiological driver.

* Ex vivo rescue. Incubation of a never-fed brain with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin drives reactivation. This shows NSCs are insulin/Dilp responsive in principle, but the supraphysiological bath bypasses normal transport, concentration and compartmentalisation and does not identify the physiological route used in vivo.

Because both ligand and binding protein freely cross the BBB a peripheral Imp-L2 sink is also a central sink. Glial sequestration feeds back on IPC Dilp2 synthesis and DRN inhibition is explicitly non-diagnostic for Dilp2 absorption. No BBB-impermeant hemolymph sink, no retrograde transport block that spares hemolymph Dilp2, and no IPC secretion-specific block that spares retrograde transport are provided. The hemolymph-secreted BBB-crossing pool and the IPC→DRN retrogradely transported pool therefore cannot be cleanly dissociated on the data given, and the data are consistent with A, B, both or neither. A clean assignment to A, B, C or D is not justified.

B. Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph

I think the fat-body Imp-L2 sink is the cleanest in vivo necessity test we have, and the BBB permeability of both ligand and binding protein actually sharpens rather than blurs the humoral reading.

Dilp2 is free to cross the BBB and Imp-L2 is free to cross the BBB. That means Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and Dilp2 present extracellularly in the brain parenchyma are in rapid equilibrium. Fat-body Imp-L2 is a secreted extracellular binding protein. It binds Dilp2 in the hemolymph, and because it itself crosses the BBB it also binds Dilp2 that is already extracellular in the brain after it has arrived from the circulation. That is exactly the signature of a humoral supply: an extracellular sink present both systemically and centrally removes the circulating-derived brain extracellular pool.

Compartment access is what distinguishes the hemolymph pool from the retrograde IPC → DRN pool for this manipulation. Retrogradely transported Dilp2 is moved intracellularly in axons and released in a largely synaptic/private compartment. Until release it is in transit intracellularly and functionally protected from an extracellular binding protein. An extracellular sink has very limited access to an in-transit intracellular pool.

If a protected intracellular retrograde pool were sufficient to drive feeding-induced NSC exit, removal of the accessible extracellular circulating pool by a fat-body sink should not be sufficient to keep NSCs quiescent despite feeding and despite IPCs being feeding induced. The fact that fat-body Imp-L2 soaking hemolymph Dilp2 blocks reactivation is most naturally read as a requirement for an extracellular-accessible pool, i.e. Dilp2 that reaches the brain from the circulation.

Imp-L2 crossing the BBB does not make the fat-body manipulation non-specific. Any Dilp2 that is extracellular in the brain after free BBB crossing is derived from the hemolymph. Imp-L2 entering the brain simply ensures that Dilp2 that has already crossed is also neutralised. That is the humoral model.

Glial Imp-L2 fits the same logic. Glial Imp-L2 is an intra-cerebral extracellular sink. It blocks reactivation and concomitantly reduces Dilp2 expression in IPCs. That is the feedback you expect if central Dilp2 signalling that normally sustains IPC output is supplied by circulating Dilp2 that has crossed the BBB: acute loss of brain extracellular Dilp2 signalling feeds back to down-regulate the source neurons, secondarily lowering both the secreted and the retrograde pools. The reduction in IPC expression is downstream of loss of systemic/central signalling, not a confound that erases the local read-out.

DRN inhibition delays reactivation, but the prompt explicitly allows DRNs a Dilp2-independent function. A DRN requirement therefore establishes a need for DRN output for timely reactivation, not that Dilp2 must be retrogradely absorbed by DRNs to drive reactivation. DRNs can act downstream of, or in parallel to, systemic Dilp2 that has reached the brain by free BBB crossing.

The ex vivo rescue with very high, non-physiological bovine insulin shows NSCs are intrinsically insulin responsive and that direct ligand access to brain tissue is sufficient in principle. In vivo that access under feeding is provided by Dilp2 secreted into the hemolymph and free to cross the BBB.

Removal of accessible circulating Dilp2 by a systemic extracellular sink that also enters the brain blocks feeding-induced reactivation, and direct brain ligand exposure is sufficient to drive it. Retrograde IPC→DRN delivery can occur, but the sink experiments show the extracellular circulating pool is the one that is required in the intact animal. The parsimonious physiological source in the fed animal is Dilp2 secreted to the hemolymph from IPCs and acting in the brain after BBB crossing.
